## Theme: `theme_blockbuster()`

Graphs in this chapter use `fmggp2::theme_blockbuster()`, modeled on a Blockbuster Video store: royal blue background, yellow ticket stub marks, white Arial text, and an Impact title.
:::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="false" icon=false}

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #02577A;"}
**Requirements:**
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"}
**✅ a numeric (continuous) variable**
:::

<br>

```{r}
#| label: full_code_display
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| out-height: '60%'
#| out-width: '60%'
#| fig-align: right
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
set.seed(1993)
blockbuster_rentals <- tibble(
  household_id = 1:60,
  rentals = rpois(n = 60, lambda = 3)
)
labs_dotplot <- labs(
  title = "Blockbuster Video",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Rentals per household in one week",
  x = "Number of rentals")
ggp2_dotplot <- ggplot(data = blockbuster_rentals,
      aes(x = rentals)) + 
    geom_dotplot(binwidth = 1, dotsize = 0.2) + 
    scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL)
ggp2_dotplot + 
  labs_dotplot
```

::::

## Description 

A dot plot displays each data point as a dot on a single axis, making it useful for identifying patterns, gaps, and outliers in small to moderate datasets. Each dot represents an observation in the data, stacked over categories or spread along a number line.

In `ggplot2`, we can build dot plots with [`geom_dotplot()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_dotplot.html)

## Set up

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**PACKAGES:**
:::


Install packages.


::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: pkg_code_dotplot
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| results: hide
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr) # for tibble() and data manipulation
```
:::



::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DATA:**
:::

In the late 90s, most Friday nights started at [Blockbuster Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blockbuster_(retailer)). 

::: {.column-margin}

![Blockbuster Video membership card (source: Wikipedia)](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/5/56/Blockbuster_membership_card.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=imageinfo&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled){fig-align="center" width="50%" height="50%"}

:::

We'll simulate how many movies 60 households rented in one week with `rpois()`, which generates whole number counts (0, 1, 2, and so on). Setting the seed with `set.seed()` means you'll get the same 60 households every time you run the code below.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: data_code_dotplot
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
set.seed(1993) # same 60 households every time the code runs
blockbuster_rentals <- tibble(
  household_id = 1:60, # 60 different households, one row each
  rentals = rpois(n = 60, lambda = 3) # weekly rentals (about 3 on average)
)
glimpse(blockbuster_rentals)
```
:::

## Distribution

Rentals are counts: a household rents 0, 1, 2, or more movies, but never 2.5. Dot plots are a good fit for counts like these because each dot is one household, so the graph is just the data stacked into piles. 

![A Blockbuster store in Durham, North Carolina (source: Wikipedia)](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/74/2008-09-24_Blockbuster_in_Durham.jpg/3840px-2008-09-24_Blockbuster_in_Durham.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=imageinfo&utm_content=thumbnail){fig-align="center" width="80%" height="80%"}

Because we picked the rental rate in `rpois()`, we know what the piles should look like before we draw them. Below we'll move from the counts, to a picture, to the formula.

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**COUNT IT:**
:::

Start with the first ten households.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: count_values_dotplot
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
head(blockbuster_rentals$rentals, 10)
```
:::

Most of these households rented two or three movies, two rented none, and one rented five. If we count all 60 households, we can compare each pile to the number of households we'd expect (we'll see where `dpois()` comes from below).

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: count_table_dotplot
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
blockbuster_rentals |> 
  count(rentals) |> 
  mutate(expected = round(60 * dpois(rentals, lambda = 3), 1))
```
:::

The observed piles stay close to the expected ones. Counts like these have one more property worth checking: the mean and the variance should be about the same.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: count_summary_dotplot
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
blockbuster_rentals |> 
  summarise(mean = mean(rentals), variance = var(rentals))
```
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**DRAW IT:**
:::

The dot plot below stacks one dot per household above its number of rentals. The tallest piles sit at two and three rentals, and the piles get shorter on both sides. The dashed line marks the rental rate we used in `rpois()` (3 per week). The right side trails out further than the left because a household can't rent fewer than zero movies.

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: draw_dotplot
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
ggplot(data = blockbuster_rentals, 
    aes(x = rentals)) + 
  geom_dotplot(binwidth = 1, dotsize = 0.3) + 
  geom_vline(xintercept = 3, linetype = "dashed", color = "white") + 
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:8) + 
  labs(x = "Number of rentals")
```
:::

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**NAME IT:**
:::

The `rpois()` call that created the data is a single statement: 

$$
X \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda = 3)
$$

The [Poisson distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_distribution) describes counts of events in a fixed window of time (here, rentals in one week). It has a single parameter, the rate ($\lambda$), which is both the mean and the variance. That's why our simulated mean (`r round(mean(blockbuster_rentals$rentals), 2)`) and variance (`r round(var(blockbuster_rentals$rentals), 2)`) are so close. 

The chance of a household renting exactly $k$ movies is:

$$
P(X = k) = \frac{\lambda^k e^{-\lambda}}{k!}
$$

This is what `dpois()` calculates. For $k = 3$, $P(X = 3) = 3^3 e^{-3} / 3! \approx 0.224$, so we'd expect about $60 \times 0.224 \approx 13$ of our 60 households to rent three movies. We got `r sum(blockbuster_rentals$rentals == 3)`. Try a larger `lambda` in `rpois()` and the piles move right and spread out, because the mean and the variance grow together.


## Grammar

::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**CODE:**
:::

1. Create labels with `labs()`

2. Initialize the graph with `ggplot()` and provide `data`

3. Map `rentals` to the `x` axis

4. Add the `geom_dotplot()` layer

5. Set the `binwidth` to `1` (one pile per count) and adjust the `dotsize`

::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}
```{r}
#| label: code_graph_dotplot
#| code-fold: show
#| eval: false
#| echo: true 
#| warning: false
#| message: false
labs_dotplot <- labs(
  title = "Blockbuster Video",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Rentals per household in one week",
  x = "Number of rentals")
ggp2_dotplot <- ggplot(data = blockbuster_rentals,
      aes(x = rentals)) + 
    geom_dotplot(binwidth = 1, dotsize = 0.2) + 
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:8) 
ggp2_dotplot + 
  labs_dotplot
```
:::


::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"}
**GRAPH:**
:::

```{r}
#| label: create_graph_dotplot
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| layout-nrow: 1
labs_dotplot <- labs(
  title = "Blockbuster Video",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Rentals per household in one week",
  x = "Number of rentals")
ggp2_dotplot <- ggplot(data = blockbuster_rentals,
      aes(x = rentals)) + 
    geom_dotplot(binwidth = 1, dotsize = 0.2) + 
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:8) 
ggp2_dotplot + 
  labs_dotplot
```


A downside of using dot plots is the lack of interpretability of the `y` axis.[^dot-y-axis] The axis is labeled `count`, but its numbers run from 0 to 1, even though the tallest pile in our graph holds 15 households.

These numbers don't line up with the piles because `geom_dotplot()` doesn't stack dots by counting them. It sizes each dot to fit the `binwidth` on the `x` axis (one rental), then stacks the dots on top of each other until the pile runs out. The height of a pile depends on how many dots it holds *and* how big each dot is, so changing `dotsize` makes every pile taller or shorter without changing the data. The `y` axis isn't measuring anything; it's just leftover space for the dots to sit in.

The number of households is still in the graph, but we read it by counting the dots in each pile, not by looking across to the axis. Because the axis can mislead readers, it's common to hide it with `scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL)`.

```{r}
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| layout-nrow: 1
labs_dotplot <- labs(
  title = "Blockbuster Video",
  caption = "Simulated data",
  subtitle = "Rentals per household in one week",
  x = "Number of rentals")
ggp2_dotplot <- ggplot(data = blockbuster_rentals,
      aes(x = rentals)) + 
    geom_dotplot(binwidth = 1, dotsize = 0.2) + 
    scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL)
ggp2_dotplot + 
  labs_dotplot
```

[^dot-y-axis]: Read more in the [function reference.](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_dotplot.html#details)
